clue.text: Your setter has succeeded as an adapter of classic French plays

definitions.text: an adapter of classic French plays

parts.note: the setter refers to themself as I, and 'has' contracts to 've
S is the abbreviation for succeeded, as in family trees

explanation.surface: The puzzle's compiler boasts of a successful career translating French stage classics.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface invites you to picture the setter as a translator; in fact 'Your setter has' is just I'VE. David Ives is an American playwright who adapted Corneille and Molière.
explanation.definitionFit: David Ives wrote modern verse versions of classic French comedies such as Corneille's The Liar.

clue.text: One reading a small part in Shakespeare

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
reading is one of the three Rs, hence R
S is the usual abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels

explanation.surface: An actor is reading for a minor role in a Shakespeare play.
explanation.definitionFit: Iras is a minor attendant on Cleopatra in Antony and Cleopatra, a small speaking role.

clue.text: Rose's work with Mark possibly playing with a lover

parts.note: St Mark is one of the four Gospel writers, an example of an evangelist
an actor playing a role appears 'as' that character
a lover of something, an enthusiast, is a fan

explanation.surface: A musician named Mark performs a piece composed by someone called Rose, alongside an admirer.
explanation.walkthrough: Rose Tremain wrote the story collection Evangelista's Fan; 'Rose' looks like a flower or a composer.
explanation.definitionFit: Evangelista's Fan is a 1994 short-story collection by the British novelist Rose Tremain.

clue.text: Which character in A Room with a View has the most quotes?

definitions.text: Which character in A Room with a View has the most quotes?

parts.words: Which character in A Room with a View has the most quotes?
parts.note: a chaperone in Forster's novel shares a surname with the famous American dictionary of familiar quotations

explanation.surface: A literary quiz question asking which figure in Forster's novel speaks the most memorable lines.
explanation.walkthrough: The question seems to ask about dialogue, but it points to Bartlett's Familiar Quotations, the standard American quotation dictionary, shared in name with Charlotte, Lucy's cousin and chaperone.
explanation.definitionFit: Charlotte is Lucy Honeychurch's fussy older cousin and chaperone in Forster's novel, and her surname names a classic quotation anthology.

clue.text: Brown bear decision is appropriate about fare

clue.text: High hill seen in part two of The Divine Comedy

indicators.note: seen in says only the part of the work's title found in its middle is wanted, the rest dropped

parts.words: part two of The Divine Comedy
parts.note: the second part of Dante's poem is Purgatorio

explanation.surface: A lofty mountain appears in the middle section of Dante's great poem.
explanation.walkthrough: The words in the clue do not themselves contain the answer: first turn 'part two of The Divine Comedy' into PURGATORIO, then find the three letters inside it. Fittingly, Purgatory is itself a mountain.
explanation.definitionFit: A tor is a high rocky hill or outcrop, especially on Dartmoor in south-west England.

clue.text: A left-winger and a visitor escaping on a bicycle follow a royal correspondent

indicators.note: follow says the pieces before it come after the royal piece in the answer

parts.note: Elizabeth is the name of queens of England
Tony Benn was a famous left-wing Labour politician

parts.words: a visitor escaping on a bicycle
parts.note: ET, the alien visitor in Spielberg's film, famously escapes flying on a bicycle

explanation.surface: A socialist and an alien on a bike tag along behind a journalist covering the monarchy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Royal correspondent' reads as a palace reporter; split it. Tony BENN was a well-known left-wing British Labour MP.
explanation.definitionFit: Austen's heroine of Pride and Prejudice exchanges letters, notably receiving Darcy's long explanatory letter, so she is a letter-writer.

clue.text: Poem from an Irishman, initially unpopular in America

indicators.note: in places the first letter inside the word for America

parts.note: America is informally called the States

indicators.note: initially picks out the opening letter of unpopular

explanation.surface: An Irish writer's poem was at first poorly received in the US.
explanation.walkthrough: Yeats wrote 'The Statues'; the surface makes 'unpopular in America' sound like a critical verdict.
explanation.definitionFit: The Statues is a late poem by W. B. Yeats, the Irish poet.

clue.text: Expert on spoken English with King's small gift finally received

parts.note: Henry is the name of many English kings, so the king's becomes Henry's
wee is Scottish for small

indicators.note: finally picks out the last letter of the word gift

explanation.surface: A language specialist accepts a modest present from the monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: Henry Sweet was the Victorian phonetician often cited as a model for Shaw's Professor Higgins.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry Sweet was a pioneering British phonetician and scholar of how English is pronounced.

clue.text: Rogue making a number one cop right busy?

clue.text: Mild oath about meeting a gnome

indicators.note: about here means turned round, so the oath is read backwards

parts.note: egad is a mild old-fashioned oath

explanation.surface: Someone mutters a gentle curse on bumping into a garden ornament.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gnome' is a garden figure in the surface but here means a pithy saying.
explanation.definitionFit: A gnome in its older sense is a short maxim or aphorism, the same as a proverb or saw.

clue.text: Modern short stories from an American author

definitions.meaning: of the present day, belonging to the current era

definitions.text: short stories from an American author

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means contemporary, and it is also the title of Ernest Hemingway's early story collection.

clue.text: Huge literary figure to pester and badger after a note that's preposterous

indicators.note: preposterous literally means back-to-front, so the whole run is reversed
after puts the pester and badger words behind the note

parts.note: ut is the old name for the first note of the scale, now doh
to nag is to pester
to rag is to tease or badger

explanation.surface: A giant from literature irritates and harasses someone, which is absurd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that's preposterous' looks like comment but is the reversal signal: preposterous comes from Latin for 'before-behind', back to front. Ut is the old name for doh.
explanation.definitionFit: Rabelais's giant Gargantua is so large that his name gave English the word for enormous.

clue.text: Adventurer that is seen between times in summer and spring

parts.note: August is a month of summer, abbreviated Aug
ie is the abbreviation for id est, that is
March is a month of spring

explanation.surface: A traveller turns up at points between summer and spring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seen between' places the IE between the two month names. Saul Bellow's novel is The Adventures of Augie March.
explanation.definitionFit: Bellow's hero is the subject of The Adventures of Augie March, a picaresque wanderer.

clue.text: Some of A Few Good Men in a court

definitions.text: Some of A Few Good Men

parts.note: CT is the abbreviation for court, as in street addresses

explanation.surface: Several characters from a courtroom drama appear before a judge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some of' looks like a hidden-word signal, but nothing is hidden: A Few Good Men is a play, and part of a play is a division of it.
explanation.definitionFit: A Few Good Men began as Aaron Sorkin's stage play, and a play is divided into acts.

clue.text: As a novel starts, she's just got hitched, with a Geordie with style reportedly

definitions.text: As a novel starts, she's just got hitched

parts.note: an is the form of a before a vowel
a Geordie is from Newcastle, in the North East, NE

indicators.note: reportedly says the word is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: to style a garment is to tailor it

explanation.surface: At the opening of a novel a woman has married a stylish man from Newcastle.
explanation.walkthrough: Emma opens just after Miss Taylor, Emma's governess, marries Mr Weston. A Geordie is a native of Newcastle upon Tyne in north-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: Austen's Emma begins with the wedding of the governess Miss Taylor, so she is newly married on page one.

clue.text: Wallace protagonist of Portuguese descent caught in dodgy saloon

indicators.note: in places the cricket letter inside the jumbled letters
dodgy suggests something unsound, so the letters of saloon are rearranged

parts.note: C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A Portuguese-born hero of a Wallace novel is arrested in a seedy bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dodgy' rearranges SALOON to NOLASO, and 'caught in' puts C inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: The hero of Edgar Wallace's story has a Portuguese surname, reflecting his family origins.

clue.text: "A potent quack, long versed in human ills (…) whose most tender mercy is —" (George Crabbe)

definitions.text: "A potent quack, long versed in human ills (…) whose most tender mercy is —" (George Crabbe)

parts.words: "A potent quack, long versed in human ills (…) whose most tender mercy is —" (George Crabbe)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation: the missing last word of the couplet from Crabbe's poem The Village about a callous parish doctor

explanation.surface: A satirical verse portrait of a heartless quack doctor, with its punchline left blank.
explanation.walkthrough: The couplet ends 'And whose most tender mercy is ...'; the word rhymes with 'protect' in the line before.
explanation.definitionFit: Crabbe's quack shows the poor no kindness at all, so his gentlest treatment is to leave them uncared for.

clue.text: Random lover returned as in this way and carried on

indicators.note: returned means the whole sequence is read back to front

parts.note: sic is Latin for thus, in this way
ran, as in ran a business, means carried on

explanation.surface: An unpredictable romantic partner came back and kept going as before.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Random' is not chance: Roderick Random is Smollett's hero. Reversed, AS SIC RAN gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: In Smollett's novel Roderick Random, the hero courts and finally marries Narcissa.

clue.text: Sculptor's letter to Gertrude

definitions.note: the clue reads 'Sculptor is', the apostrophe s being a contraction of the verb, so the noun alone is the definition and still matches a single person

parts.note: Ep. is the abbreviation for epistle, a letter
Gertrude Stein was the American modernist writer

explanation.surface: An artist writes a note to the writer Gertrude Stein.
explanation.walkthrough: Jacob Epstein was the American-born British sculptor.
explanation.definitionFit: Jacob Epstein was a major twentieth-century modernist sculptor working in Britain.

clue.text: I'm OK re the problematic American poet

indicators.note: problematic suggests something in disorder, so those letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A speaker insists they are fine about the troublesome American poet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'problematic' rearranges OK RE THE; 'I'm' only sets up the surface. Theodore Roethke was a Pulitzer-winning American poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Theodore Roethke was a twentieth-century American poet who won the Pulitzer Prize.

clue.text: Short stories in Kanarese

indicators.note: in signals that the letters sit inside the next word

explanation.surface: Brief tales written in a south Indian language.
explanation.walkthrough: Kanarese is an old name for Kannada, a language of south India.
explanation.definitionFit: Ana are collections of anecdotes or table talk about a person, a crossword-friendly word.

clue.text: Violently hate tripe that Harold Robbins wrote

indicators.note: violently suggests the letters are thrown about and rearranged

explanation.surface: A reader fiercely loathes the trash a bestselling novelist produced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Violently' rearranges HATE TRIPE; the surface poses as a critic's verdict on a popular novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pirate is a 1974 bestselling novel by the American author Harold Robbins.

clue.text: What solvers may need to do some time before this puzzle ends

definitions.text: What solvers may need to do

indicators.note: before puts the time word ahead of the final letters

parts.note: an era is a period of time

indicators.note: ends picks out the last letter of each of the words this and puzzle

explanation.surface: A remark that solvers may have to rub out entries just before finishing.
explanation.definitionFit: A solver who has written a wrong entry must rub it out with an eraser.

clue.text: Ring up a meliphagous character

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: a hoop is a ring

explanation.surface: Someone telephones a honey-eating figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ring up' looks like making a phone call. Meliphagous means honey-eating, which points to Milne's bear.
explanation.definitionFit: Winnie-the-Pooh is A. A. Milne's bear, famously addicted to honey.

clue.text: What sounds like a story play or biography with style

definitions.text: What sounds like a story play

parts.note: a biography is a life of someone
class means style or elegance

explanation.surface: A theatrical or written account of someone's life done elegantly.
explanation.walkthrough: A life class is an art class drawing from a nude model; read as words it suggests a course on life stories, a playful definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Taken literally, a lesson about lives sounds like drama about a story, though it is a drawing class with a model.

clue.text: Jonathan Cape initially offered Introduction to Economics

indicators.note: initially picks the first letter of each of the words Cape and offered
an introduction to a word is its opening letter

explanation.walkthrough: Jonathan Cape is a London publishing house; the surface uses it as a publisher, but only Cape gives a letter and Jonathan is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Jonathan Coe is the English novelist of What a Carve Up! and The Rotters' Club.

clue.text: Detailed description of part of Switzerland found in The Divine Comedy

parts.note: Switzerland is divided into cantons

explanation.walkthrough: 'Detailed description' looks like a full account; read as de-tailed it cuts N from CANTON.
explanation.definitionFit: Dante's poem is divided into one hundred cantos, so a canto is a section within it.

clue.text: A short rhyme that's curiously redolent

indicators.note: curiously suggests an odd arrangement, so the letters are reworked

explanation.surface: A brief poem that is strangely evocative.
explanation.definitionFit: A rondelet is a short French verse form of seven lines with a refrain.

clue.text: Ancient creator of typescript — a hack?

explanation.surface: Who wrote this typescript — some hired writer?
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across the end of 'typescript' and 'a hack'. 'Hack' looks like a poor writer, which suits the surface's creator.
